lesson.title: The Reliable Workhorse: How TCP Makes the Internet Trustworthy
lesson.summary: TCP is the connection-oriented transport layer protocol that turns an unreliable IP network into what looks, from an application's point of view, like a reliable, ordered stream of bytes.
lesson.body:
TCP is the other major transport layer protocol alongside UDP, and it does the same basic port based job of getting data to the right process on the right host, but it builds a great deal of additional machinery on top of that basic job. It was originally standardized in RFC 793 in 1981 and has since been clarified and consolidated in RFC 9293, one more example of how a foundational internet protocol is anchored to a written specification rather than to any single implementation.

Where UDP is connectionless, TCP is connection oriented, and that single difference is the root of nearly everything else that sets the two protocols apart. Before either side of a TCP conversation can exchange a single byte of application data, both sides must complete an explicit setup step, the three way handshake, that establishes shared state, most importantly each side's own starting point for counting bytes. Everything else TCP does depends on that shared state existing first.

On top of that connection state, TCP builds three main guarantees. It delivers data reliably and in order, using sequence numbers and acknowledgment numbers to detect gaps and duplicates and to trigger retransmission when something is missing. It protects the receiver from being overwhelmed through flow control, where the receiver continuously advertises how much buffer space it currently has so the sender never sends faster than the receiver can absorb. And it ends a conversation through an explicit, multi step termination sequence rather than simply going silent. Each of these pieces gets its own closer look in the chapters that follow.

The reason any of this exists at all is that the network underneath, IP, makes no delivery promises whatsoever: packets can be dropped, duplicated, or delivered out of order by routers along the way, and IP itself does nothing to fix any of that. TCP exists specifically to hide that unreliability from the application, presenting what looks like a single continuous, ordered, dependable stream of bytes between two processes, so that a web browser, an email client, or a file transfer tool does not have to reinvent retransmission and reordering logic on its own every time.

That reliability is not free. All the extra state and bookkeeping mean TCP carries more overhead per connection than UDP, and it costs at least one round trip of setup time before any application data can flow at all. That cost is exactly why UDP continues to exist as the other option, for the cases willing to skip the setup and tolerate some loss in exchange for lower latency.
